clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous, usually de novo, loss-of-function variants in KMT2A (formerly MLL/MLL1), a histone methyltransferase that deposits activating methyl marks on lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4)
Hypertrichosis cubiti, or prominent hair over the elbows, is a well-known clue although it is not present in every child
Thick or arched eyebrows, long eyelashes and generalised hypertrichosis accompany a recognisable facial appearance with hypertelorism and downslanting palpebral fissures
Developmental delay and intellectual disability of variable severity are core features, frequently with short stature and muscular hypotonia
Feeding difficulties in infancy, recurrent infections and behavioural or autistic features are commonly reported
A KMT2A-specific DNA methylation episignature is increasingly used to confirm the diagnosis and to clarify variants of uncertain significance
As a chromatinopathy affecting an H3K4 methyltransferase, it belongs to the same broad family as other Mendelian disorders of the epigenetic machinery
reference.pathophysiology: KMT2A encodes a histone methyltransferase that catalyses methylation of histone H3 at lysine 4, a modification associated with open, transcriptionally active chromatin at gene promoters and enhancers. Loss-of-function variants reduce the enzyme's dose (haploinsufficiency), blunting the deposition of these activating marks and disturbing the precise programmes of gene expression required for growth and neurodevelopment. The consequent dysregulation of developmental gene networks yields the characteristic pattern of intellectual disability, growth restriction, hypertrichosis and craniofacial features, and because the defect produces a reproducible genome-wide methylation signature it can be detected by episignature testing.
additionalDifferentials: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (NIPBL and related genes)
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to identify KMT2A variants
DNA methylation episignature analysis to confirm the diagnosis or resolve uncertain variants
Neurodevelopmental, cognitive and behavioural assessment including autism screening
Growth monitoring and evaluation of short stature
Immunological review if recurrent infections are prominent
redFlags: Significant feeding difficulty with faltering growth in infancy
Recurrent or severe infections suggesting immune dysfunction
Developmental regression, which is atypical and warrants reassessment
reference.prognosis: The disorder is compatible with survival into adulthood; intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate but ranges more widely, and most individuals benefit substantially from early developmental, educational and behavioural support, with growth and feeding issues tending to improve after infancy.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because hypertrichosis cubiti is absent, when the feature is inconstant
Mislabelling the child as Cornelia de Lange or Kabuki syndrome without gene-specific or episignature testing
Overlooking recurrent infections that may reflect immune involvement
Dismissing behavioural and autistic features that benefit from targeted intervention
references: Nature Reviews Genetics — chromatinopathies and histone methylation disorders
